analysis.one_liner: Adds foreclosure protections and oversight for homeowners with FHA-insured mortgages.
analysis.headline: The FHA Foreclosure Prevention Act was introduced in April 2018, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required companies that service FHA-insured mortgages to document that they followed federal loss-mitigation rules (options to avoid foreclosure) before collecting an FHA insurance payout, created a public complaint and appeal process for borrowers, barred foreclosures while a borrower complaint was pending, and required detailed written notices explaining why a borrower was denied help. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners with FHA-insured mortgages who fall behind on payments. The bill would make it harder for servicers to foreclose without first offering foreclosure-prevention options, give borrowers a way to complain and appeal directly to HUD, and stop a foreclosure while a complaint or appeal was being decided [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires mortgage servicers to document compliance with loss-mitigation (foreclosure-avoidance) requirements before HUD pays them an insurance claim, and preserves HUD's ability to impose civil monetary penalties [S3].

Directs HUD to regularly oversee FHA mortgage servicers, sample and review their compliance, and take corrective action against non-compliant servicers, including barring foreclosure and cancelling interest and fees that accrued during periods of noncompliance [S3].
Creates a borrower complaint procedure at HUD for servicing and loss-mitigation problems, with an appeal process, and prohibits foreclosure while a complaint or appeal is pending [S3].

Requires written notice to borrowers before foreclosure acceleration explaining how loss-mitigation options were evaluated, why the borrower was found ineligible, and how to file a complaint or appeal [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers and the lenders who hold FHA-insured mortgages, who would face documentation requirements, HUD oversight and corrective actions, clawbacks of fees accrued during noncompliance, and a ban on foreclosing while a borrower complaint is pending [S3]. Taxpayers could also bear indirect costs if FHA insurance claims are delayed or foreclosure timelines stretch [S3].

drawbacks.text: The prohibition on foreclosing during any pending complaint or appeal, plus a reasonable period afterward, could extend foreclosure timelines significantly and raise costs for lenders and for the FHA insurance fund [S3].

Requiring documentation before any insurance claim is paid could delay claim payments to lenders and add compliance costs for servicers, costs that could be passed on to borrowers through servicing fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For FHA borrowers at risk of losing their homes, the protections are concrete: a foreclosure pause during disputes, a right to see why they were denied help, and servicer accountability before insurance claims are paid. The costs fall mainly on servicers, though longer foreclosure timelines and slower insurance claims could raise costs for the FHA fund that taxpayers ultimately back. On balance the bill was a borrower-protection measure with modest, well-identified costs to industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2018 and stayed there; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the FHA Foreclosure Prevention Act of 2018 on April 18, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced [S5].
No other action was ever taken on the bill; it received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and FHA lenders came out ahead: the documentation requirements, fee clawbacks, HUD oversight, and foreclosure prohibitions that would have applied to them never became law, and foreclosures on FHA borrowers continued under the pre-existing rules.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the FHA Foreclosure Prevention Act of 2018; no other member signed on.

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee took no action on it — no hearing or markup was scheduled during the 115th Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 18, 2018 and never reported it out; the bill's only recorded action after introduction was the referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4]; its sponsor was the senior Democrat on the committee whose Republican chairman never acted on it, so the bill never attracted bipartisan or committee support.

industries.note: The bill would have conditioned FHA insurance payouts on documented compliance with foreclosure-avoidance rules, clawed back interest and fees accrued during noncompliance, and barred foreclosure while a borrower complaint was pending [S3]. Servicers' interest in collecting fees and completing foreclosures quickly ran directly against the borrowers the bill protected.
